title: Chrismation and confirmation
hookLine: the Orthodox anoint babies right after baptism; many Western churches confirm in youth

lines: A PROPHET WITH A HORN OF OIL.
THE YOUNGEST, IN FROM THE SHEEP.
cards: An old prophet walks into Bethlehem carrying a horn full of oil. He's come to the house of a man named Jesse to find a king.
One son after another is brought before him, tall, strong, impressive, and each time the answer is no. Is there anyone else? Well, the youngest.
He's out with the sheep. They send for him, and the boy comes in from the field.
"Then Samuel took the horn of oil, and anointed him in the midst of his brethren: and the Spirit of the LORD came upon David from that day forward." Oil on the head, and the Spirit comes.

teach.b: Chrism is oil set apart for anointing. In Orthodox and Catholic practice it's olive oil with fragrance mixed in, blessed by a bishop. It's the oil of the step that follows baptism, and here the churches split on timing.

A baby comes up out of the water and, in the same service, the priest touches the oil to forehead, eyes, nostrils, lips, ears, chest, hands and feet, saying the words of the rite: the seal of the gift of the Holy Spirit.
They call it chrismation. The baby is then a full member, and can come to the table. In the West, Catholics, and some Anglicans and Lutherans among others, usually separate the two.
A child is baptized as a baby and confirmed years later, often by a bishop, who lays on hands and anoints with chrism. They call it confirmation.
Some other Protestant churches keep a confirmation without oil, as a time to learn the faith and say yes to it, and some have no such rite at all. Both ways point back to the same pages.
In Acts, Peter and John come to new believers who had been baptized, and "laid they their hands on them, and they received the Holy Ghost."
Paul packs it into two verses: God "hath anointed us," and "hath also sealed us, and given the earnest of the Spirit in our hearts."
A seal was pressed into wax to say: this belongs to someone, and it's been closed with care. Same oil. Different clocks.

how: Orthodox Christians are anointed with chrism, chrismation, in the same service as baptism, even as infants; Catholics and some other Western churches confirm later, with the laying on of hands and, in Catholic practice, anointing with chrism.

o: the white robe worn after a baptism
blessed, fragrant oil used to anoint and seal
holy water used to bless a new church building

games.q: you're Samuel. Jesse's tall, impressive sons have all passed in front of you, and none is the one. what do you do?
o: ask if there's anyone else, and wait for the youngest.
go home with the horn still full.
games.why: the youngest is out with the sheep. they send for David, and Samuel anoints him "in the midst of his brethren."

practice: Touch a little oil or lotion to the inside of your wrist, or just press two fingers there, where you can feel your pulse. Notice the smell, if there is one, and the beat under your fingers.
If you pray, say Paul's words slowly, anointed, sealed; if not, keep your fingers on your pulse and count a few beats.

wordCard.voice: Chrism. Blessed, fragrant oil, used to anoint and seal: right after baptism for the Orthodox, at confirmation for some Western churches.

orig.note: Greek: an anointing, oil for anointing — the word behind "unction" in 1 John 2:20.

carryVoice: Your line: sealed. In the old picture, a seal means kept with care, not locked away. Until tomorrow.
